# Waiting and risk

## Waiting time for the next exceedance, by hand

$\tau$ is the number of years until the "coin" next comes up "heads".
By the geometric distribution:

$$
p_\tau(k) = (1-p)^{k-1} p, \qquad E[\tau] = \frac{1}{p} = T
$$

## Waiting time for the next exceedance, by simulation

$p = 0.01$

::: {.cell execution_count=1}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1}
![](return-periods-julia_files/figure-typst/cell-4-output-1.svg){}
:::
:::



## How variable is that wait?

$$
\mathrm{Var}(\tau) = \frac{1-p}{p^2}, \qquad \mathrm{sd}(\tau) = \frac{\sqrt{1-p}}{p} \approx T \text{ for small } p
$$

The spread is as large as the mean wait, so the mass near 1 and the long tail are the same picture.

::: {.cell execution_count=1}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1}
![](return-periods-julia_files/figure-typst/cell-5-output-1.svg){}
:::
:::



## How likely are two exceedances in ten years, at $p = 1/4$?

Ten flips of the bent coin, so $N = 10$, with $Y$ the number of heads.

$$
p_Y(y) = \binom{N}{y} p^y (1-p)^{N-y}
$$

::: {.cell execution_count=1}
``` {.julia .cell-code}
Y = Binomial(10, 0.25)
p_two_or_more = 1 - pdf(Y, 0) - pdf(Y, 1)
@printf("P(Y >= 2) = %.3g", p_two_or_more)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
P(Y >= 2) = 0.756
```
:::
:::



A "4-year flood" turns up at least twice per decade more often than not.

## Rarer events: $p = 1/10$

Same ten flips, same count $Y$, a coin bent one tenth of the way instead of one quarter.

::: {.cell execution_count=1}
``` {.julia .cell-code}
Y = Binomial(10, 0.1)
p_two_or_more = 1 - pdf(Y, 0) - pdf(Y, 1)
@printf("P(Y >= 2) = %.3g", p_two_or_more)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
P(Y >= 2) = 0.264
```
:::
:::



We get two "ten-year floods" in a decade a quarter of the time.

## What risk does a design life carry?

$$
R = 1 - (1-p)^N, \qquad T = \frac{1}{1 - (1 - R)^{1/N}}
$$

::: {.cell execution_count=1}
``` {.julia .cell-code}
risk(T, N) = 1 - (1 - 1 / T)^N
T_needed(R, N) = 1 / (1 - (1 - R)^(1 / N))

@printf("100-year flood, 50-year life: R = %.3g\n", risk(100, 50))
@printf("10%% risk over a 5-year job needs T = %.3g years", T_needed(0.10, 5))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
100-year flood, 50-year life: R = 0.395
10% risk over a 5-year job needs T = 48 years
```
:::
:::

::: {.cell execution_count=1}

### Which axis is data, and which is an estimate?

- Level: a number a gauge recorded.
- Return period: computed from the rank of that level in a finite record.

:::
:::

## How is the return period estimated?

Sort descending, so rank $i = 1$ is the largest, and a hat marks a quantity computed from the record rather than known.

$$
\hat p_i = \frac{i}{n + 1}, \qquad \hat T_i = \frac{1}{\hat p_i}
$$

Over $n$ years an event with annual probability $p$ is exceeded about $np$ times, so a value exceeded $i$ times out of $n$ estimates $\hat p \approx i/n$.
Dividing by $n+1$ instead gives the Weibull plotting position.
